questions.question: Explain why gold mining on the Witwatersrand needed large companies and capital from the start.
questions.expected_answer: The gold, found on the farm Langlaagte in 1886, was in fine particles in hard conglomerate rock called banket, not in riverbed gravels that individuals could wash. It was low-grade, so huge tonnages had to be mined and crushed; it was deep, because the reef sloped steeply underground from the outcrop, so deep-level mines were needed; and below a certain depth it was locked in pyrite, needing the MacArthur-Forrest cyanide process introduced in 1890. Stamp batteries, cyanide plants, winding engines, pumps and compressors cost far more than individual diggers could afford, so mining houses raised capital by selling shares to investors in London, Paris and Berlin.

questions.question: Who were the Randlords and what was the basis of their power?
questions.expected_answer: The Randlords were the small group of very wealthy men who controlled the gold mines through mining houses: Cecil John Rhodes and Charles Rudd with Gold Fields of South Africa from 1887; Alfred Beit and Julius Wernher with the Corner House of Hermann Eckstein, with Lionel Phillips; Barney Barnato; Joseph Robinson; George Farrar, Abe Bailey and others. Many came from Kimberley with experience of raising capital and controlling labour. Their power was economic, controlling an industry that produced more than a quarter of the world's gold by the late 1890s; social, with grand houses in Parktown and London; and political, with links to the British government and the press. They differed politically: some, like Robinson, worked with Kruger; others, like Rhodes and the Corner House, opposed him.

questions.question: Explain why the Chamber of Mines was formed and how it tried to control costs and influence the government.
questions.expected_answer: Formed in 1887 and reorganised in 1889, the Chamber let mining companies act together. Because the gold price was fixed internationally, rising costs cut profits and could close low-grade mines. Labour was the largest cost, so the Chamber agreed maximum black wages in 1890 and 1896, cut black wages in 1896, and set up recruiting bodies, the Rand Native Labour Association in 1896 and WNLA from 1900 to 1901, recruiting across southern Africa and especially southern Mozambique, to stop mines competing for workers. It lobbied the Kruger government against the costly dynamite concession, high railway rates and liquor sales to workers, and for stricter pass laws, obtaining a mining-district pass law in 1895. The Randlords' conflict with Kruger contributed to the Jameson Raid and the South African War.
